artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider subsets $A\subseteq \mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}$ satisfying
$$\sum_{(x,y)\in A,\ (x,y)\neq(0,0)} \frac{1}{x^2+y^2} = \infty.$$
(a) Must every such set $A$ contain the four vertices of an axis-aligned square, i.e. four points of the form $(x,y),\ (x+d,y),\ (x,y+d),\ (x+d,y+d)$ for some $x,y\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $d\in\mathbb{N}$?
(b) More generally, must every such set $A$ contain a $k\times k$ axis-aligned square grid $\{(x+id,y+jd):0\le i,j\le k-1\}$ for every integer $k\ge 2$?
artifact.status_search_result: No published proof or disproof of this two-dimensional analogue of Graham's conjecture (a planar version of the Erdős–Graham-type problem on arithmetic configurations in sets with divergent reciprocal-sum weights) was located. The problem appears to remain open, and Graham's monetary prize for its resolution has not been recorded as claimed.
